summary: Queue consumer for a bucket's object-create notifications that writes a sidecar file, named by a hash of the object key, back into the same bucket, where the notification rule has no prefix or suffix filter.

also.contains: async queue(batch: MessageBatch<ObjectEvent>, env: Env): Promise<void> {
npx wrangler r2 bucket notification create clipshare-media --event-type object-create --queue media-events

expected_findings.explanation: scripts/setup.sh creates an object-create rule on clipshare-media with no --prefix or --suffix, so every new object in the bucket sends a message to media-events. The consumer answers each message by writing a sidecar into the same bucket, at meta/<SHA-256 of the key>.json. The sidecar is a new object and raises the same event, and the consumer does not skip keys under meta/, so the next message writes a sidecar for the sidecar, and so on. Every sidecar key is 74 bytes long, so R2's 1,024-byte limit on key length never stops the chain (a key that grew on each pass would stop there after about a hundred objects). One upload starts a chain that never ends, each link costing about three queue operations, an R2 read, an R2 write and a stored object, with no user involved. The rule lives outside the Wrangler config, in the setup script.

may_flag.reason: Separate from the loop: uploads are kept forever with no total per user, and the only limit is 20 uploads a minute per user, counted per location. The size check defaults a missing Content-Length to 0, so 25 MiB is not even a ceiling. At 25 MiB, one account from one location adds 864,000 uploads, about 21 TiB a month, about $316 a month of R2 storage that recurs and grows, so a report may rate it High (v28).
